function:
def f(n: int, x: int, y: int, m: int) -> tuple:
    flag = x < y * m
    if flag:
        p = n // x
        q = p * y
        r = n - p * x
        u = r // m
        val = q + u
    else:
        u = n // m
        p = 0
        val = u
    d = {"used_rope": flag, "rope_units": p, "direct_torches": u}
    return val, d
description:
INPUTS: You start with four whole numbers: n, x, y, and m. Think of each of these as just a numeric value that you can add, multiply, divide, and compare with the others. There’s no list or text – just these four integers sitting in front of you. 

LOGICS: Alright, what you’re going to do first is decide whether to take the left path or the right path. To do that, multiply y by m. After you get that product, look at your x and ask: is x strictly smaller than that product? Write down that comparison result as a true-or-false marker called flag.  

If flag is true (meaning x < y · m):  
  1. You’re going to see how many full chunks of size x you can fit into n. To find that, do integer division of n by x (ignore any remainder) and call the result p.  
  2. Next, you want to figure out a temporary total by scaling p up by y. So multiply p times y and call that q.  
  3. Then find out what’s left over in n after removing those p chunks of size x. Calculate r = n – (p · x).  
  4. Now check how many full chunks of size m you can take out of the remainder r. Do integer division of r by m and call that u.  
  5. Finally, add that u to your earlier q to get your overall tally val = q + u.  

If flag is false (meaning x ≥ y · m):  
  1. You skip the step with p altogether and just figure out how many full chunks of size m you can fit into n. So do integer division of n by m and call that u.  
  2. Since you didn’t use any x-sized chunks, set p = 0.  
  3. Your overall tally val is simply the value you just got for u.  

At this point, regardless of which path you took, you have three numbers:  
  • flag (true or false),  
  • p (the count of x-sized chunks you used),  
  • u (the count of m-sized chunks you used),  
  • and val (the final total you calculated).  

Gather these into a little record called d, with three entries:  
  • used_rope: flag  
  • rope_units: p  
  • direct_torches: u  

Then you’re done. You return the pair: first the number val, and then the record d. 

OUTPUTS: In the end, you’ll have two things:  
1. A single integer val – that’s your combined total from whichever steps you took.  
2. A dictionary d with exactly three entries:  
   • used_rope: a true/false flag telling you which branch you ran.  
   • rope_units: the integer p, showing how many times you used the x-sized chunks (or 0 if you didn’t).  
   • direct_torches: the integer u, showing how many times you used the m-sized chunks.  

That pair (val, d) is exactly what the function would hand back if you did it by hand.

INPUTS: You’re working with three whole-number values called n, m, and val. Think of n and m as two integers you multiply together to get a workspace size, and val as another integer you want to check against that size and see how it divides into n or m. 

LOGICS: Okay, here’s how you do it step by step. First, what you’re going to do is multiply n by m and call that result x. So take your n and m, multiply them, and write down x = n * m. Next, set up a stats dictionary with two entries: early_exit starts at 0, and orientation_checks starts at 0. Now you need to see if val is bigger than x. So compare val to x. If val is greater than x, then set stats["early_exit"] to 1, and you’re done—you return False along with your stats. That ends the process early. If val is not greater than x (meaning val ≤ x), you keep going. At this point, you’re about to do your first orientation check, so add 1 to stats["orientation_checks"]. Now check whether val divides evenly by n: compute val modulo n and see if the remainder is zero. If the remainder is zero, that means val divides by n without leftover. In that case, figure out y by dividing val by n. Then check if y falls between 1 and m−1 inclusive—that is, make sure 1 ≤ y < m. If that condition holds, you return True and your stats right away. If either the modulo test failed or the y check failed, you move on. Next, you’re doing your second orientation check, so add 1 more to stats["orientation_checks"]. Now test whether val divides evenly by m: compute val modulo m and see if that remainder is zero. If it is zero, then compute z by dividing val by m. Then verify that z is between 1 and n−1 inclusive—so check 1 ≤ z < n. If that’s true, return True and stats. If not, or if the modulo wasn’t zero, then none of the checks succeeded, so you finally return False along with the stats dictionary. 

OUTPUTS: In the end you get two things: a True/False result and the stats dictionary. The True/False tells you whether either of those division-and-bounds checks passed. In stats, early_exit will be 1 if you quit right away because val was too big (otherwise it stays 0), and orientation_checks will be how many of those two division checks you actually performed (it will be 0, 1, or 2 depending on whether you exited early or passed one of the tests).

LOGICS: First, lay out your workspace by writing down the three integer inputs n, m, and k. Next, create a stats dictionary with two entries named loop_iterations and segment_completions, both set to zero. Now, check whether k is equal to 1. If it is, what you’re going to do is multiply n and m to get your final value right away and stop—return that product together with your stats (which remain at zero). If k is not 1, you define a helper routine that processes a single integer x as follows:

- Start by setting a = 1 and b = 0.
- Then, for each y counting from 1 up to x (inclusive):
  - Immediately increase the counter loop_iterations in your stats by 1.
  - Set a temporary variable new_b equal to the current value of b.
  - Check if y is at least k:
    - If yes, increase the counter segment_completions in stats by 1, and add the value of a to new_b.
  - After that decision, overwrite b with new_b.
- Once you’ve gone through all y values up to x, the helper returns the final value of b.

After you’ve got that helper in place, go back to the main steps: call it with x = m and multiply its returned b by n; then call it again with x = n and multiply its returned b by m; finally, add those two products together to get your overall result. At that point, return that sum along with the stats dictionary, which has been accumulating counts during both helper runs. 

OUTPUTS: You end up with two things: 1) a single integer—the sum of n times the helper’s result on m plus m times the helper’s result on n—and 2) your stats dictionary. In that dictionary, loop_iterations tells you how many times you ran through the counting loop in total, and segment_completions tells you how many times y met or exceeded k and triggered an addition to b.

description:
INPUTS: L is a list of pairs of integers (x, y). You also create an empty dictionary mp that will map integers to integers, a dictionary d with two counters 'find_calls' and 'path_updates' both set to 0, and an empty list arr to collect results. 

LOGICS: First, you set up your workspace by creating an empty dictionary called mp to store links between numbers, then another dictionary called d with two counters 'find_calls' and 'path_updates' both set to 0, and finally an empty list called arr for the results. Now what you're going to do is define a helper named fn that takes a single number u. At the very start of fn, add 1 to d['find_calls']. Then check if u is not in mp. If it's not there, set mp[u] equal to u itself and return u right away. Otherwise, find the root: set a variable root equal to u and then, while mp[root] is not equal to root, set root equal to mp[root]. At this point, root holds the ultimate link. Next you're going to flatten the path: set current equal to u and then while mp[current] is not equal to current, do the following: first let nxt equal mp[current], then set mp[current] to root, then add 1 to d['path_updates'], and finally set current to nxt. When that loop ends, return root from fn. With fn in place, you move on to processing your list L. Now you need to go through each pair (x, y) in L in order. For each pair, figure out m by taking x plus y minus 1, then dividing that sum by y using integer division to drop any remainder, and then multiplying the quotient by y to get the smallest multiple of y that's at least x. What you do next is call fn on that m and call its output val. Immediately append val to arr. Then call fn again on val plus y, take that second output, and store it in mp at key val by setting mp[val] equal to that second output. That way you've set up the next link. You repeat exactly those steps for every (x, y). When there are no more pairs left, you're done. 

OUTPUTS: At the end you have arr, which is a list of integers (one entry per original pair in L), and d, a dictionary where 'find_calls' is the total number of times you entered fn and 'path_updates' is the total number of times you reassigned a link in mp during your path-flattening steps.

function:
def f(n, A, B):
    from bisect import bisect_left
    lst = sorted(zip(A, B), key=lambda v: v[0])
    A = [u for u, _ in lst]
    B = [v for _, v in lst]
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)
    stats = {'improvements': 0, 'eliminations': 0}
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + 1
        x, y = A[i - 1], B[i - 1]
        val = x - y
        j = bisect_left(A, val)
        option = dp[j] + 1
        if option < dp[i]:
            dp[i] = option
            stats['improvements'] += 1
            stats['eliminations'] += (i - 1) - j
    return dp[n], stats

INPUTS: You start with three inputs: n is a single integer telling you how many entries there are; A is a list of n numbers; and B is another list of n numbers. You can assume A and B are the same length and all entries are numeric. 

LOGICS: What you’re going to do is start by creating a list called lst that pairs each A[k] with its matching B[k] for k from 0 up to n-1. Next, sort lst in increasing order of the first element in each pair. Once that’s done, rebuild A as the list of those first elements in sorted order and rebuild B as the list of those second elements. Now set up a new list dp of length n+1 and initialize every entry to zero. Also make a stats record with two counters: improvements set to 0 and eliminations set to 0.

Now you begin a loop where i runs from 1 through n. At the start of each iteration, set dp[i] = dp[i-1] + 1. Then look at x = A[i-1] and y = B[i-1], and compute val = x - y. Your next task is to find a position j in A between 0 and n such that A[j] is the first entry greater than or equal to val and all earlier entries are smaller than val. To do that, scan A from index 0 upward until you hit an entry that is at least val; if none qualifies all the way to the end, let j = n. Once you know j, calculate option = dp[j] + 1. If option is less than dp[i], that means you’ve found an improvement: set dp[i] = option, add 1 to your improvements counter, and add (i - 1 - j) to your eliminations counter. If option is not smaller, leave dp[i] and stats alone. Then move on to the next value of i. Continue until you have processed i = n. 

OUTPUTS: When you finish the loop, you end up with two things. The first is the number dp[n], which is the final numeric result after processing all n items. The second is your stats record: improvements tells you how many times you replaced dp[i] with a strictly better option, and eliminations tells you the total number of positions you skipped over each time you applied one of those improvements.

def f(n, A, B):
    from bisect import bisect_left
    lst = sorted(zip(A, B), key=lambda v: v[0])
    A = [u for u, _ in lst]
    B = [v for _, v in lst]
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)
    stats = {'improvements': 0, 'eliminations': 0}
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + 1
        x, y = A[i - 1], B[i - 1]
        val = x - y
        j = bisect_left(A, val)
        option = dp[j] + 1
        if option < dp[i]:
            dp[i] = option
            stats['improvements'] += 1
            stats['eliminations'] += (i - 1) - j
    return dp[n], stats

INPUTS: a single integer called n 

LOGICS: What you're going to do is first set up two counters named loop_iters and adjust, both starting at 0. Now look at your integer n and ask: is n less than or equal to 0? If it is, you stop right there and you know your result will be 0, with loop_iters still at 0 and adjust still at 0. If n is not less than or equal to 0, the next thing you check is: is n exactly 1? If it is, you stop again, but this time your result is 6, and your counters are still loop_iters = 0 and adjust = 0.

If neither of those two quick checks applies (so n is greater than 1), you move on. What you do is compute a value called val by taking n, multiplying by 12, and then subtracting 3. Next, you set up a small workspace: put x = 0, y = val, and root = 0.

Now you begin a loop that keeps going as long as x is less than or equal to y. At the top of that loop, add 1 to your loop_iters counter. Then find the midpoint m by adding x and y together and dividing by 2, ignoring any remainder (integer division). After that, square m to get p (so p = m times m).

Next, compare p to val: if p equals val exactly, set root to m and break out of the loop entirely. If p is less than val, that means your midpoint squared is too small, so set root to m and then move your lower bound up by setting x to m + 1. Otherwise (meaning p is greater than val), your midpoint squared is too big, so move your upper bound down by setting y to m - 1. Then loop back and repeat: check x versus y, increment loop_iters, compute a new midpoint, square it, and adjust x or y or break if you hit the exact square.

When that loop finishes—either because you broke out on an exact match or because x climbed above y—do one more check: multiply root by itself and see if it's still less than val. If it is, that means you need to round up one more step. So add 1 to root and set adjust to 1. If root squared is not less than val, leave root and adjust alone (adjust stays 0).

Finally, take your root value, double it to get your final result, and you’re done. You’ll hand back that result number along with the two counters loop_iters (how many times you went through the while loop) and ceil_adjustments (which is 1 if you had to bump root up, or 0 if you didn’t). 

OUTPUTS: You end up with two things: first, a single number called result, which is twice the integer root you found; and second, a small dictionary of statistics where loop_iters tells you how many iterations of the loop you performed, and ceil_adjustments tells you whether you performed one final increase of root (it’s 1 if you did that, or 0 if you didn’t).

**Function Description:**  
INPUTS: You start off with two inputs. First, there’s n, which is just a single whole number. Second, there’s lst, which is a list where each item is itself a pair of whole numbers (we’ll call those x and y). 

LOGICS: Okay, let’s walk through every little thing step by step. What you’re going to do is treat n as the size of your workspace and lst as a sequence of pairs you need to handle one by one.

1. First thing, set up a constant called mod and give it the value 998244353. You won’t change this; it’s just sitting there for the very last step.
2. Create two counters: one named edge_iterations and another named vertex_iterations. Start both of them at zero. These will keep track of how many times you do two different loops.
3. Build an array A that has exactly n+1 slots, and put a zero in every slot. So A[0] is zero, A[1] is zero, all the way up to A[n] is zero. (You’ll only use 1 through n, but this makes indexing easy.)

4. Now you need to go through each pair in lst in order. I’ll call the current pair x and y:
   - Before you do anything else in this loop, add 1 to edge_iterations.
   - Then go look at A[x] and add 1 to that slot.
   - Next, look at A[y] and add 1 to that slot.
   - Right after you bump those two, check: if A[x] is now greater than 2 or A[y] is now greater than 2, you must stop everything and return out = 0. Along with that zero, you hand back your two counters in a dictionary like {'edge_iterations': current_edge_iterations, 'vertex_iterations': current_vertex_iterations}. That ends the whole process immediately.
   - If neither A[x] nor A[y] went above 2, keep going to the next pair in lst until you’ve processed them all.

5. At this point, you’ve survived the first loop without exceeding 2 on any A-slot. Now set up two more placeholders: val = 0 and val2 = 0. These will hold small tallies based on what’s in A.
6. Next, go through the numbers i = 1, 2, 3, …, up to n, one by one:
   - Each time you start a new i, add 1 to vertex_iterations.
   - Look at A[i]. If A[i] is 0 or 1 (that is, A[i] <= 1), do the following:
     * Add 1 to val.
     * Then, if A[i] is exactly 1, also add 1 to val2. (If A[i] is 0, you do not touch val2.)
   - If A[i] is 2 or higher, you don’t change val or val2; you just move on.

7. After that second loop finishes, you’ve got two numbers: val (how many slots were 0 or 1) and val2 (how many slots were exactly 1).
8. Now do some arithmetic:
   - Compute m = val * (val – 1) // 2. (That’s integer division after multiplying.)
   - Compute res = m * (m – 1) // 2.
   - Compute res2 = val2 * ((val – 1) * (val – 2) // 2).
9. Figure out your final output number out by taking (res – res2) and then reducing it modulo your mod (998244353). In other words, out = (res - res2) % mod.

• edge_iterations: how many pairs (x, y) from lst you processed before either quitting early or finishing them all.    
• vertex_iterations: how many times you looked at slots A[1] through A[n] in that second loop.   
If you ever hit a situation where A[x] or A[y] went above 2 in the first loop, out will be 0 and the dictionary shows how many iterations of each kind you did up to that point.

INPUTS: You start with a list called L that has n items, where each item is itself a pair of numbers. In other words, L is a list of length n, and each element of L is two numbers (we’ll call them x and y when we pick one item). 

LOGICS: First, figure out how many items are in L and call that number n. Next, create an empty dictionary called mp where you’ll keep counts of certain sums—whenever you look up a key that isn’t already in mp, pretend its count is zero, then you’ll increment it. Also, make a variable named pair_iterations and set it to zero; that will track how many pairs you process.

Now you’re going to compare every pair of items in L exactly once. So do this: for i running from 0 up to n−1, take the item at position i and call its two numbers x and y. Then, inside that, run another index j from i+1 up to n−1. For each j, look at the item at position j and call its two numbers u and v. What you do next is:
 1. Figure out sumX by adding x and u.
 2. Figure out sumY by adding y and v.
 3. In your mp dictionary, find the entry for the key (sumX, sumY). If it doesn’t exist yet, treat it as zero, then add 1 to that count and store it back in mp.
 4. Add 1 to your pair_iterations counter.

Keep doing that inner loop over j until you’ve paired i with every later item, then go back and increment i and repeat. When both loops finish, mp holds a count for every possible (sumX, sumY) you saw, and pair_iterations tells you how many pairs you went through in total.

At this point, you need to extract two final summary values. Start by setting active_midpoints to zero and val to zero. Next, look at each count value in mp (call each one cnt). For each cnt:
 - If cnt is greater than 1, that means this particular (sumX, sumY) happened more than once, so add 1 to active_midpoints.
 - Then compute cnt * (cnt − 1) and divide that by 2 (dropping any remainder) and add the result to val.

Do that for every cnt in mp. When you’re done, you have val, active_midpoints, and the original pair_iterations. 

OUTPUTS: After these steps, you end up with two things. First, a number val, which is the sum over every mp count of cnt * (cnt − 1) / 2 (using integer division). Second, a dictionary of two statistics: “pair_iterations” is the total count of all i,j pairs you processed, and “active_midpoints” is how many distinct (sumX, sumY) keys had a count above 1.

def f(n, x, A):
    val = A[x-1]
    lst = [A[i] for i in range(x-1) if A[i] < val]
    lst.sort(reverse=True)
    y = len(lst)
    B = [0] * (y + 1)
    for i in range(y):

    m = sum(A[:x-1])
    u, v, w = 0, y, y
    c = 0
    while u <= v:
        c += 1
        t = (u + v) // 2
        if B[t] + t >= m:
            w = t
            v = t - 1
        else:
            u = t + 1
    d = {'eligible_count': y, 'sum_eligible': B[y], 'binary_search_steps': c}
    return w, d

def f(n, d, L, B):
    import heapq
    arr = [0] * n
    y = 0
    lst = []
    left = 0
    c1 = 0
    c2 = 0
    c3 = 0
    for i in range(n):
        while left < i and L[i] - L[left] > d:
            left += 1
            c1 += 1
        while lst and lst[0][1] < left:
            heapq.heappop(lst)
            c2 += 1
        z = 0
        if lst:
            t = -lst[0][0]
            u = t + d - L[i]
            z = u if u > 0 else 0
        if z > 0:
            c3 += 1
        arr[i] = B[i] + z
        y = arr[i] if arr[i] > y else y
        heapq.heappush(lst, (-(arr[i] + L[i]), i))
    return y, {'num_left_advances': c1, 'num_heap_pops': c2, 'num_non_zero_extensions': c3}

For each item, which we’ll call x, add 1 to sim_iters—that’s tracking each inner step.  Next, compute d by subtracting y from x.  If d is greater than zero, check if val is smaller than d. If instead d is zero or negative, you take the negative of d (so you’re actually getting |d|), add that to val, and then if val ever grows larger than your original m, set it back down to m.  After dealing with d, set y to the current x and move on to the next element in A.  Once you’ve handled every element without returning False, g returns True.  Now, back in the main work: first check if n is zero or A is empty.  If either of those is true, you skip all the searching and simply return 0 along with your two counters.  If you do have data, set lo equal to 0 and hi equal to the largest number found in A.  Also set ans equal to that same hi.  Now you run a loop as long as lo is less than or equal to hi.  At the top of each loop, add 1 to bs_iters—this is tracking each binary‐search step.  Then figure out x by taking lo plus hi and dividing by two, dropping any fraction.     from collections import Counter
    mp = {}
    d = Counter(L)
    A = sorted(d.keys())
    d2 = {}
    res = 0
    c = 0
    n = 0
    m = 0
    k = 0
    for v in A:

        d2[v] = tot
        if tot > res:
            res = tot
        pairs = tot // 2
        k += pairs
        c = pairs
        n += 1
    x = A[-1] + 1 if A else 0
    while c > 0:
        tot = c
        d2[x] = tot
        if tot > res:
            res = tot
        pairs = tot // 2
        k += pairs
        c = pairs
        x += 1
        m += 1
    mp['unique_levels'] = n
    mp['carry_levels'] = m
    mp['merge_pairs'] = k
    return res, mp

def f(n, par, L, C, lst):
    A = [[] for _ in range(n+1)]
    for y in range(2, n+1):
        p = par[y]
        A[p].append(y)
    B = [0] * (n+1)
    for y, cnt in lst:
        if 1 <= y <= n and cnt > 0:
            B[y] += cnt
    H = [0] * (n+1)
    res = 0
    shipments_moved = 0
    warehouses_opened = 0
    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    def dfs(x):
        nonlocal res, shipments_moved, warehouses_opened
        f_x = B[x]
        for y in A[x]:
            H[y] = H[x] + L[y]
            f_y = dfs(y)
            shipments_moved += f_y
            res += f_y * L[y]
            f_x += f_y
        if x != 1 and f_x * H[x] > C[x]:
            res += C[x]
            warehouses_opened += 1
            f_x = 0
        return f_x
    dfs(1)
    return res, {'shipments_moved': shipments_moved, 'warehouses_opened': warehouses_opened}

function:
def f(n, par, L, C, lst):
    A = [[] for _ in range(n+1)]
    for y in range(2, n+1):
        p = par[y]
        A[p].append(y)
    B = [0] * (n+1)
    for y, cnt in lst:
        if 1 <= y <= n and cnt > 0:
            B[y] += cnt
    H = [0] * (n+1)
    res = 0
    shipments_moved = 0
    warehouses_opened = 0
    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    def dfs(x):
        nonlocal res, shipments_moved, warehouses_opened
        f_x = B[x]
        for y in A[x]:
            H[y] = H[x] + L[y]
            f_y = dfs(y)
            shipments_moved += f_y
            res += f_y * L[y]
            f_x += f_y
        if x != 1 and f_x * H[x] > C[x]:
            res += C[x]
            warehouses_opened += 1
            f_x = 0
        return f_x
    dfs(1)
    return res, {'shipments_moved': shipments_moved, 'warehouses_opened': warehouses_opened}

def f(n, par, L, C, lst):
    A = [[] for _ in range(n+1)]
    for y in range(2, n+1):
        p = par[y]
        A[p].append(y)
    B = [0] * (n+1)
    for y, cnt in lst:
        if 1 <= y <= n and cnt > 0:
            B[y] += cnt
    H = [0] * (n+1)
    res = 0
    shipments_moved = 0
    warehouses_opened = 0
    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    def dfs(x):
        nonlocal res, shipments_moved, warehouses_opened
        f_x = B[x]
        for y in A[x]:
            H[y] = H[x] + L[y]
            f_y = dfs(y)
            shipments_moved += f_y
            res += f_y * L[y]
            f_x += f_y
        if x != 1 and f_x * H[x] > C[x]:
            res += C[x]
            warehouses_opened += 1
            f_x = 0
        return f_x
    dfs(1)
    return res, {'shipments_moved': shipments_moved, 'warehouses_opened': warehouses_opened}

def f(n, arr):
    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    stats = {"recursive_calls": 0, "elements_processed": 0}
    def dc(x, y):
        stats["recursive_calls"] += 1
        if y - x + 1 <= 32:
            sm = 0
            mx = 0
            for i in range(x, y + 1):
                stats["elements_processed"] += 1
                val = arr[i]
                sm += val
                if val > mx:
                    mx = val
            return sm, mx
        m = (x + y) // 2
        sm_l, mx_l = dc(x, m)
        sm_r, mx_r = dc(m + 1, y)
        total = sm_l + sm_r
        maximum = mx_l if mx_l > mx_r else mx_r
        return total, maximum
    if n < 2:
        return 0, stats
    total, maximum = dc(0, n - 1)
    bound1 = total // 2
    bound2 = total - maximum
    result = bound1 if bound1 < bound2 else bound2
    return result, stats

def f(arr):
    A = sorted(set(arr))
    n = len(A)
    mp = {v: i+1 for i, v in enumerate(A)}
    B = [0] * (n + 1)
    comp_count = n
    upd_steps = 0
    sel_steps = 0
    def add(i, delta):
        nonlocal upd_steps
        while i <= n:
            B[i] += delta
            upd_steps += 1
            i += i & -i
    def kth(k):
        nonlocal sel_steps
        idx = 0
        bit_mask = 1 << (n.bit_length() - 1)
        while bit_mask > 0:
            sel_steps += 1
            t = idx + bit_mask
            if t <= n and B[t] < k:
                idx = t
                k -= B[t]
            bit_mask >>= 1
        return idx + 1
    res = []
    cnt = 0
    for x in arr:
        add(mp[x], 1)
        cnt += 1
        k = (cnt + 1) // 2
        pos = kth(k)
        res.append(A[pos - 1])
    stats = {'uniq_count': comp_count, 'update_steps': upd_steps, 'select_steps': sel_steps}
    return res, stats

INPUTS: arr is a list of numbers. 

LOGICS: Start by taking your array named arr. Write down every number you see, then cross out duplicates until each appears only once. Sort the remaining numbers in ascending order and call the result A. Count how many items are in A and call that n. Next, build a mapping mp so that each value v in A maps to its one-based index: go through A in order with an index i starting at zero and set mp[v] = i + 1 for each.
Then create a list B of length n + 1 and fill it with zeros (you will use positions 1 through n). After that, set comp_count = n, upd_steps = 0, sel_steps = 0.

What you're going to do now is define two helper routines:

1) add(i, delta):
   While i <= n:
     - Add delta to B[i].
     - Add 1 to upd_steps.
     - Compute lowbit as i & -i (the lowest set bit in i).
     - Set i = i + lowbit.
   End while.

2) kth(k):
   - Set idx = 0.
   - Compute bit_mask as the largest power of two <= n by taking the bit length of n minus one and doing 1 << that.
   - While bit_mask > 0:
       * Add 1 to sel_steps.
       * Let t = idx + bit_mask.
       * If t <= n and B[t] < k:
           - Subtract B[t] from k.
           - Set idx = t.
       * Right-shift bit_mask by 1 (bit_mask >>= 1).
     End while.
   - Return idx + 1.

At this point, set res = [] and cnt = 0. Now go through each x in your original arr, in order:
  1. Let i = mp[x].
  2. Call add(i, 1).
  3. Increase cnt by 1.
  4. Compute k = (cnt + 1) // 2.
  5. Call kth(k) and call its result pos.
  6. Append A[pos - 1] to res.

Once you've processed all x, build stats = {'uniq_count': comp_count, 'update_steps': upd_steps, 'select_steps': sel_steps}. The function then returns (res, stats).

def f(arr):
    A = sorted(set(arr))
    n = len(A)
    mp = {v: i+1 for i, v in enumerate(A)}
    B = [0] * (n + 1)
    comp_count = n
    upd_steps = 0
    sel_steps = 0
    def add(i, delta):
        nonlocal upd_steps
        while i <= n:
            B[i] += delta
            upd_steps += 1
            i += i & -i
    def kth(k):
        nonlocal sel_steps
        idx = 0
        bit_mask = 1 << (n.bit_length() - 1)
        while bit_mask > 0:
            sel_steps += 1
            t = idx + bit_mask
            if t <= n and B[t] < k:
                idx = t
                k -= B[t]
            bit_mask >>= 1
        return idx + 1
    res = []
    cnt = 0
    for x in arr:
        add(mp[x], 1)
        cnt += 1
        k = (cnt + 1) // 2
        pos = kth(k)
        res.append(A[pos - 1])
    stats = {'uniq_count': comp_count, 'update_steps': upd_steps, 'select_steps': sel_steps}
    return res, stats

def f(arr):
    A = sorted(set(arr))
    n = len(A)
    mp = {v: i+1 for i, v in enumerate(A)}
    B = [0] * (n + 1)
    comp_count = n
    upd_steps = 0
    sel_steps = 0
    def add(i, delta):
        nonlocal upd_steps
        while i <= n:
            B[i] += delta
            upd_steps += 1
            i += i & -i
    def kth(k):
        nonlocal sel_steps
        idx = 0
        bit_mask = 1 << (n.bit_length() - 1)
        while bit_mask > 0:
            sel_steps += 1
            t = idx + bit_mask
            if t <= n and B[t] < k:
                idx = t
                k -= B[t]
            bit_mask >>= 1
        return idx + 1
    res = []
    cnt = 0
    for x in arr:
        add(mp[x], 1)
        cnt += 1
        k = (cnt + 1) // 2
        pos = kth(k)
        res.append(A[pos - 1])
    stats = {'uniq_count': comp_count, 'update_steps': upd_steps, 'select_steps': sel_steps}
    return res, stats

You also need three counters before you begin looping: set m equal to 0, support_checks equal to 0, and dp_updates equal to 0.

     -  If A[h] is bigger than y, you do nothing and move on to the next smaller h.

INPUTS: You have arr, which is a list of sequences. Each item in arr, called s, is itself a sequence (for example a list or string) of elements that can be compared for equality. That is the only input. 

LOGICS: Start by creating an empty list called A. Then set val to zero – that will track the total number of adjacent pairs that differ across all sequences – and set y to zero – that will count how many sequences contain at least one equal adjacent pair.

Now go through each sequence in arr one at a time, naming the current one s. First, find out how many elements are in s by counting them; call that number n. Next, set x to zero; x will measure how many adjacent pairs in s differ.

Next, check every adjacent pair in s by starting with an index i at zero and then moving up to i = n - 2. At each step, compare the element at s[i] with s[i+1]. If they’re not equal, add 1 to x. Keep doing this until you’ve compared all pairs from the first position up to the next-to-last one. After that loop, x holds the count of differing adjacent pairs in s.

Now decide if there’s any adjacent pair in s that are the same. To do that, set a flag variable called flag to False. Then loop with i from 0 up to n - 2 again. At each i, check if s[i] is equal to s[i+1]. If you find a match, set flag to True and immediately stop this loop. That tells you there’s at least one pair of identical neighbors.

After checking for equal neighbors, look at flag. If flag is True, that means s had at least one equal adjacent pair. In that case, add 1 to y. Then calculate z by taking x and adding 2, but because you can't have more adjacent positions than n - 1, if z becomes greater than n - 1, set z to n - 1. If flag is False, simply set z equal to x.

Next, append z to the list A, and also add x to val. That way, you accumulate your results as you move from one sequence to the next. Keep going until you’ve processed all sequences in arr. Once you’re done, A is fully built, val holds the total of all x values, and y counts how many sequences had at least one equal adjacent pair. 

OUTPUTS: You end up with A, which is a list of numbers (one for each sequence in arr) representing the z value you computed for that sequence. You also get a stats dictionary with two entries: diff_pairs, which is the total val (the sum of x counts across all sequences), and improvable_count, which is y (the number of sequences that had at least one adjacent pair of equal elements).

def f(n, arr, lst):
    parent = list(range(n+2))
    rem = [0] + arr[:]
    d = {'find_calls': 0, 'while_iters': 0, 'merges': 0}
    def find(x):
        d['find_calls'] += 1
        if parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = find(parent[x])
        return parent[x]
    A = []
    for x, val in lst:
        idx = find(x)
        rem_val = val
        while idx <= n and rem_val > 0:
            d['while_iters'] += 1
            if rem[idx] >= rem_val:
                rem[idx] -= rem_val
                rem_val = 0
                if rem[idx] == 0:
                    parent[idx] = find(idx+1)
                    d['merges'] += 1
                break
            rem_val -= rem[idx]
            rem[idx] = 0
            parent[idx] = find(idx+1)
            d['merges'] += 1
            idx = parent[idx]
        A.append(rem_val)
    return A, d

INPUTS: You have three things to write down: 1) A single number n, 2) A list called arr that has exactly n numbers in it, and 3) A list called lst that contains pairs of numbers – each pair looks like (x, val). Here x is an integer index and val is another integer. 

LOGICS: Alright, let's walk through it step by step. What you're going to do is process those inputs by hand exactly the same way the function would.

1. Setting up your workspace:
   - First, write down n.  
   - Then create a list called parent that goes from 0 up to n+1. In other words, parent[0] = 0, parent[1] = 1, parent[2] = 2, …, up to parent[n+1] = n+1.  
   - Next, make a list called rem that also goes from index 0 to index n. Put a 0 in rem[0], and then copy arr’s first element into rem[1], arr’s second element into rem[2], and so on until rem[n] holds arr[n-1].  
   - Now write down a small dictionary of counters d = { 'find_calls': 0, 'while_iters': 0, 'merges': 0 }.  
   - Finally, get an empty list A ready; this is where you’ll store your outputs one by one.

2. Defining how to find the current representative of an index (the find operation):
   Whenever I say "call find on x," do this by hand:
   a. Add 1 to d['find_calls'].  
   b. Look at parent[x]. If parent[x] == x, you’re done: the representative is x.  
   c. If parent[x] != x, you need to find parent[x]’s representative. So you call find on parent[x], which again adds to your find_calls. Once you get that result, overwrite parent[x] with the result (this is path compression), and then return it.  

3. Now process each pair in lst one by one:
   For each pair (x, val) in your lst, do this:
   a. Start by calling find(x). That gives you an index idx.  
   b. Set a temporary number rem_val = val.  
   c. Now you enter a loop that keeps going as long as idx is at most n AND rem_val is greater than zero:
      - First thing in the loop: add 1 to d['while_iters'].

def f(n, arr, lst):
    parent = list(range(n+2))
    rem = [0] + arr[:]
    d = {'find_calls': 0, 'while_iters': 0, 'merges': 0}
    def find(x):
        d['find_calls'] += 1
        if parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = find(parent[x])
        return parent[x]
    A = []
    for x, val in lst:
        idx = find(x)
        rem_val = val
        while idx <= n and rem_val > 0:
            d['while_iters'] += 1
            if rem[idx] >= rem_val:
                rem[idx] -= rem_val
                rem_val = 0
                if rem[idx] == 0:
                    parent[idx] = find(idx+1)
                    d['merges'] += 1
                break
            rem_val -= rem[idx]
            rem[idx] = 0
            parent[idx] = find(idx+1)
            d['merges'] += 1
            idx = parent[idx]
        A.append(rem_val)
    return A, d

def f(n, A):
    prev = [-1] * n
    nxt = [n] * n
    st = []
    l_pops = 0
    for i in range(n):
        while st and A[st[-1]] <= A[i]:
            st.pop()
            l_pops += 1
        prev[i] = st[-1] if st else -1
        st.append(i)
    st.clear()
    r_pops = 0
    for i in range(n-1, -1, -1):
        while st and A[st[-1]] < A[i]:
            st.pop()
            r_pops += 1
        nxt[i] = st[-1] if st else n
        st.append(i)
    total = n * (n + 1) // 2
    balanced = 0
    for i in range(n):
        x = i - prev[i]
        y = nxt[i] - i
        balanced += x + y - 1
    return total - balanced, {'left_pops': l_pops, 'right_pops': r_pops, 'balanced_subarrays': balanced}

  1. While st is not empty AND A at the index on top of st is strictly less than A[i], pop the top index off st and add 1 to r_pops.

    nxt = [n] * n
    st = []
    l_pops = 0
    for i in range(n):
        while st and A[st[-1]] <= A[i]:
            st.pop()
            l_pops += 1
        prev[i] = st[-1] if st else -1
        st.append(i)

    for i in range(n-1, -1, -1):

            r_pops += 1

        st.append(i)

def f(n, A):
    prev = [-1] * n
    nxt = [n] * n
    st = []
    l_pops = 0
    for i in range(n):
        while st and A[st[-1]] <= A[i]:
            st.pop()
            l_pops += 1
        prev[i] = st[-1] if st else -1
        st.append(i)
    st.clear()
    r_pops = 0
    for i in range(n-1, -1, -1):
        while st and A[st[-1]] < A[i]:
            st.pop()
            r_pops += 1
        nxt[i] = st[-1] if st else n
        st.append(i)
    total = n * (n + 1) // 2
    balanced = 0
    for i in range(n):

         – Add 1 to x.
         – Keep repeating.
     • As soon as you see no entry or a count less than 2, exit the loop.

def f(n, arr, lst):
    import heapq
    edge_count = 0
    push_count = 0
    pop_count = 0
    L = [0] * n
    for x, y in lst:
        edge_count += 1
        L[x - 1] += 1
        L[y - 1] += 1
    B = [val - 1 for val in L]
    h = []
    for i in range(n):
        if B[i] > 0:
            heapq.heappush(h, (-arr[i], i))
            push_count += 1
    res = []
    total = sum(arr)
    res.append(total)
    for _ in range(n - 2):
        neg_w, idx = heapq.heappop(h)
        pop_count += 1
        total += -neg_w
        res.append(total)
        B[idx] -= 1
        if B[idx] > 0:
            heapq.heappush(h, (neg_w, idx))
            push_count += 1
    return (res, {'edge_count': edge_count, 'push_count': push_count, 'pop_count': pop_count})

Now you’re going to walk through every pair in lst one at a time. For each pair, call its two entries x and y. Each time you handle one pair, add 1 to edge_count. Then go to position x minus 1 in your L list and add 1 there. After that, go to position y minus 1 in L and add 1 there as well. That finishes processing that pair, so move on until all pairs are done. 

At this point, L holds a count in each slot. The next thing is to make a new list called B, also with n slots. To fill B, look at each slot in L in order from the first to the nth: take its number, subtract 1, and write the result into the corresponding slot in B. 

Now set up an empty list called h. You’ll treat h like a priority queue by always keeping it sorted so that the smallest first element in each pair sits at the front. After that, go through each index i from 0 up to n minus 1. For each i, look at B[i]. If B[i] is greater than zero, you create a pair whose first part is the negative of arr[i] (that is, -arr[i]) and whose second part is i, then insert that pair into h and re-sort h so the smallest pair leads. Every time you insert, add 1 to push_count.

def f(n, arr, lst):
    import heapq
    edge_count = 0
    push_count = 0
    pop_count = 0
    L = [0] * n
    for x, y in lst:
        edge_count += 1
        L[x - 1] += 1
        L[y - 1] += 1
    B = [val - 1 for val in L]
    h = []
    for i in range(n):
        if B[i] > 0:
            heapq.heappush(h, (-arr[i], i))
            push_count += 1
    res = []
    total = sum(arr)
    res.append(total)
    for _ in range(n - 2):
        neg_w, idx = heapq.heappop(h)
        pop_count += 1
        total += -neg_w
        res.append(total)
        B[idx] -= 1
        if B[idx] > 0:
            heapq.heappush(h, (neg_w, idx))
            push_count += 1
    return (res, {'edge_count': edge_count, 'push_count': push_count, 'pop_count': pop_count})

def f(n, arr, lst):
    import heapq
    edge_count = 0
    push_count = 0
    pop_count = 0
    L = [0] * n
    for x, y in lst:
        edge_count += 1
        L[x - 1] += 1
        L[y - 1] += 1
    B = [val - 1 for val in L]
    h = []
    for i in range(n):
        if B[i] > 0:
            heapq.heappush(h, (-arr[i], i))
            push_count += 1
    res = []
    total = sum(arr)
    res.append(total)
    for _ in range(n - 2):
        neg_w, idx = heapq.heappop(h)
        pop_count += 1
        total += -neg_w
        res.append(total)
        B[idx] -= 1
        if B[idx] > 0:
            heapq.heappush(h, (neg_w, idx))
            push_count += 1
    return (res, {'edge_count': edge_count, 'push_count': push_count, 'pop_count': pop_count})

def f(n, m, a, b, lst):
    import bisect
    lst1 = []
    lst2 = []
    for x, y in lst:
        if x == a:
            lst1.append(y)
        if y == b:
            lst2.append(x)
    lst1.sort()
    lst2.sort()
    inf = 10**18
    i1 = bisect.bisect_right(lst1, b)
    r_obs = lst1[i1] if i1 < len(lst1) else inf
    l_obs = lst1[i1 - 1] if i1 > 0 else -inf
    i2 = bisect.bisect_right(lst2, a)
    d_obs = lst2[i2] if i2 < len(lst2) else inf
    u_obs = lst2[i2 - 1] if i2 > 0 else -inf
    d_r = (m - b) if r_obs == inf else (r_obs - b - 1)
    d_l = (b - 1) if l_obs == -inf else (b - l_obs - 1)
    d_d = (n - a) if d_obs == inf else (d_obs - a - 1)
    d_u = (a - 1) if u_obs == -inf else (a - u_obs - 1)
    filtered_candidates = len(lst1) + len(lst2)
    free_directions = (1 if d_r > 0 else 0) + (1 if d_l > 0 else 0) + (1 if d_d > 0 else 0) + (1 if d_u > 0 else 0)
    orig = True if (a == 1 or a == n or b == 1 or b == m) else (d_r > 0 or d_l > 0 or d_d > 0 or d_u > 0)
    return orig, {"filtered_candidates": filtered_candidates, "free_directions": free_directions}

def f(n, m, a, b, lst):
    import bisect
    lst1 = []
    lst2 = []
    for x, y in lst:
        if x == a:
            lst1.append(y)
        if y == b:
            lst2.append(x)
    lst1.sort()
    lst2.sort()
    inf = 10**18
    i1 = bisect.bisect_right(lst1, b)
    r_obs = lst1[i1] if i1 < len(lst1) else inf
    l_obs = lst1[i1 - 1] if i1 > 0 else -inf
    i2 = bisect.bisect_right(lst2, a)
    d_obs = lst2[i2] if i2 < len(lst2) else inf
    u_obs = lst2[i2 - 1] if i2 > 0 else -inf
    d_r = (m - b) if r_obs == inf else (r_obs - b - 1)
    d_l = (b - 1) if l_obs == -inf else (b - l_obs - 1)
    d_d = (n - a) if d_obs == inf else (d_obs - a - 1)
    d_u = (a - 1) if u_obs == -inf else (a - u_obs - 1)
    filtered_candidates = len(lst1) + len(lst2)
    free_directions = (1 if d_r > 0 else 0) + (1 if d_l > 0 else 0) + (1 if d_d > 0 else 0) + (1 if d_u > 0 else 0)
    orig = True if (a == 1 or a == n or b == 1 or b == m) else (d_r > 0 or d_l > 0 or d_d > 0 or d_u > 0)
    return orig, {"filtered_candidates": filtered_candidates, "free_directions": free_directions}

    lst2 = []
    for x, y in lst:

            lst1.append(y)

            lst2.append(x)

    lst2.sort()

    i1 = bisect.bisect_right(lst1, b)
    r_obs = lst1[i1] if i1 < len(lst1) else inf

    d_l = (b - 1) if l_obs == -inf else (b - l_obs - 1)

    d_u = (a - 1) if u_obs == -inf else (a - u_obs - 1)

INPUTS: You’ve got two things to start with: an integer called n that tells you how many items are in your list, and a list named A that has exactly n entries. You can think of A as just a row of values (they could be numbers, text, whatever—just treat them as items you’ll count and compare). 

LOGICS: Start by setting up a dictionary called stats with three counters all at zero: 'calls', 'key_iters', and 'merge_ops'.  

Now check: if n is 0 or 1, there’s no real work to do—just return 0 for your main result and hand back stats as-is.  

Otherwise, you’re going to run a little procedure, which we’ll call helper, on the whole range of your list. You invoke helper with x = 0 and y = n.  

Inside helper you do the following steps every time you enter it:  
1. Add 1 to stats['calls'].  
2. Look at the size of the current slice by computing y minus x. If that value is 1 or less, you’re down to a slice of size 1 (or empty). In that case:  
   • Build a tiny map (call it mp) with a single entry: the item A[x] as the key and 1 as its count.  
   • Return that map and 0 (because there are no pairs to count in a single item).  
3. If y – x is bigger than 1, you split it:  
   • Compute m as the integer midpoint, (x + y) // 2.  
   • Call helper(x, m) and save its outputs as mp1 and c1.  
   • Call helper(m, y) and save its outputs as mp2 and c2.  
4. After you’ve got those two maps and two counts, figure out how many items were in each half:  
   • n1 = m – x  
   • n2 = y – m  
5. You’re going to count how many pairs are equal across the two halves. First, add the number of keys in mp1 to stats['key_iters']—this tracks how many key checks you do in total. Then set eq = 0 and do this:  
   • For each key k with count v in mp1, look up k in mp2 (if it’s missing, treat it as zero).  
   • Multiply v by that mp2 count and add the result to eq.  
6. Compute cu = n1 * n2 – eq. That tells you how many cross‐pairs are unequal.  
7. Next, you merge mp1 and mp2 into one combined map. To keep it efficient, compare their sizes:  
   • If mp1 has fewer entries than mp2, call mp2 your big map (mp_big) and mp1 your small map (mp_small).  
   • Otherwise, mp1 is mp_big and mp2 is mp_small.  
8. Add the size of mp_small to stats['merge_ops']—that tracks how many individual entries you merged.  
9. Then go through every key k with count v in mp_small and do this:  
   • In mp_big, set its count for k to mp_big.get(k, 0) + v.  
10. Finally return two things from helper: mp_big (the merged map) and the sum c1 + c2 + cu (your running total of unequal pairs so far).  

When helper finishes running on the full range 0 to n, you’ll get back a merged map (which you can ignore) and a number total. That total is the main result f hands you, combined with the stats dictionary that’s been collecting counts all the way through. 

OUTPUTS: When you’re all done, you’ll end up with two things:  
1. A single number, which is the total of every c1 + c2 + cu you computed across all splits—that’s your final output value.  
2. The stats dictionary, whose three entries mean:  
   • 'calls': how many times you entered the helper procedure (including every tiny slice).  
   • 'key_iters': the total count of keys you looped over when comparing the two halves for equal items.  
   • 'merge_ops': the total number of individual map entries you merged when combining those halves.  
Together, that number and the stats dictionary give you exactly what the function would return if you ran it in code.

def f(n, arr, Q):
    A = list(range(n+1))
    B = [0] * (n+1)
    C = [0] * n
    C[0] = 0
    find_calls = 0
    def g(x):
        nonlocal find_calls
        while A[x] != x:
            find_calls += 1
            A[x] = A[A[x]]
            x = A[x]
        find_calls += 1
        return x
    D = sorted(arr, key=lambda z: z[2])
    m = 0
    for x, y, val in D:
        ru = g(x)
        rv = g(y)
        if ru == rv:
            continue
        A[rv] = ru
        y = 2 * val
        B[ru] = max(B[ru], B[rv], B[ru]//2 + B[rv]//2 + y)
        m += 1
        C[m] = max(C[m-1], B[ru])
        if m == n - 1:
            break
    lst = []
    for y in Q:
        if y >= n:
            lst.append(0)
        else:
            lst.append(C[n-1-y]//2)
    return lst, {"find_calls": find_calls, "queries_count": len(Q)}

    find_calls = 0

            find_calls += 1
            A[x] = A[A[x]]
            x = A[x]
        find_calls += 1
        return x
    D = sorted(arr, key=lambda z: z[2])
    m = 0
    for x, y, val in D:
        ru = g(x)
        rv = g(y)
        if ru == rv:
            continue
        A[rv] = ru
        y = 2 * val
        B[ru] = max(B[ru], B[rv], B[ru]//2 + B[rv]//2 + y)
        m += 1
        C[m] = max(C[m-1], B[ru])
        if m == n - 1:
            break
    lst = []
    for y in Q:
        if y >= n:
            lst.append(0)
        else:
            lst.append(C[n-1-y]//2)
    return lst, {"find_calls": find_calls, "queries_count": len(Q)}

LOGICS: What you're going to do is work through these numbers in a few clear steps.  

1. Sort A into a new list called B.  So you look at all the numbers in A and rearrange them in increasing order and call that sorted list B.  

2. Build a list C of the gaps between neighbors in B.  You go from i = 0 up to the second-to-last index of B.  For each i, you compute C[i] = B[i+1] minus B[i].  When you're done, C has one fewer element than B.  

3. Check if C is empty.  If B had 0 or 1 item, then there are no gaps and C is empty.  In that case you stop right here and you return out = 0, oversized_gaps = 0, query_steps = 0.  Otherwise, keep going.  

4. Find s, the size of your tree base.  Start with s = 1.  While s is less than the length of C, double it (s = s * 2).  When that loop finishes, s is the smallest power of two that’s at least as big as the number of gaps in C.  

5. Make an array T of length 2 * s and fill every entry with 0.  We’ll use this for a simple tree structure.  

6. Initialize a counter c1 = 0.  This will track how many gaps are "oversized."  

7. Now go through each gap in C by its index i (from 0 up to len(C) - 1):  
   - Let val = C[i].  
   - If val is greater than m, then compute t = floor((val - 1) / m).  That tells you how many extra pieces you need.  Put T[s + i] = t, and then add 1 to your oversized counter c1.  
   - Otherwise (val ≤ m), just leave T[s + i] = 0.  

8. Build the upper levels of the tree in T.  For each j from s - 1 down to 1 (in descending order), set T[j] = T[2*j] + T[2*j + 1].  You're summing two child slots into their parent.  

9. Prepare to do a full-range query.  Set another counter cnt = 0.  This will count how many times you enter the main loop of your query.  

10. Define the query process over an interval [l, r]:  
    a. Start res = 0.  
    b. Shift your interval into the tree level by doing l = l + s and r = r + s.  
    c. While l ≤ r, do these steps:  
       i.   Add 1 to cnt (this logs that you're about to inspect one or two tree slots).  
       ii.  If l is odd, add T[l] to res and then do l = l + 1.  
       iii. If r is even, add T[r] to res and then do r = r - 1.  
       iv.  After those checks, shrink the interval by doing l = l // 2 and r = r // 2.  
    d. When l passes r, exit the loop and return res.  

11. Finally, call that query with l = 0 and r = len(C) - 1.  Store its return value in out.  

12. You’re done.  Return out as your main result, and also hand back a little dictionary with two entries: 'oversized_gaps': c1 and 'query_steps': cnt.

At the same time, make two dictionaries: d1 maps n to 0, and d2 maps m to 0.  

Now go into a loop that runs while st1 is not empty. Inside that loop, the very first thing is to compare the sizes of st1 and st2. If st1 has more items than st2, swap the contents of st1 with st2, and swap d1 with d2 too. After you do that swap, add 1 to stats['swaps'].  

Right after handling a possible swap, you’re starting a new search level—so add 1 to stats['levels']. Then create an empty set called st3; this will collect the next wave of values. Now, for each element x in st1, do the following: look up x in d1 and call that number val. Then consider two candidate values for y: one is x minus 1, the other is x times 2. If y is not in d2, then record y in this dictionary by setting d1[y] = val + 1, add y into your set st3, and also add 1 to stats['nodes'].  

After you’ve done both candidate values for every x in st1, replace st1 with st3 and loop back to check if st1 is empty. If you ever exit the loop because st1 has no items left, it means you never found a meeting point: in that case, return -1 together with your stats as they stand.

def f(n, A, B):
    D = sorted(set(A))
    ubc = len(D)
    C = []
    m = 0
    for d in D:
        val1 = d - m - 1
        if val1 > 0:
            C.append(val1)
        m = d
    if n - m > 0:
        C.append(n - m)
    sc = len(C)
    C.sort(reverse=True)
    E = sorted(enumerate(B), key=lambda t: t[1], reverse=True)
    F = [0] * len(B)
    x = 0
    y = 0
    i = 0
    sw = 0
    for d1, val in E:
        while i < len(C) and C[i] >= val:
            x += C[i]
            y += 1
            i += 1
            sw += 1
        F[d1] = x - y * (val - 1)
    return F, {"unique_broken_count": ubc, "segment_count": sc, "sweep_steps": sw}

def f(n, m, x, y, lst):
    import heapq
    A = [[] for _ in range(n+1)]
    for a, b, val, lst2 in lst:
        lst2 = sorted(lst2)
        A[a].append((b, val, lst2))
    INF = float('inf')
    arr = [INF] * (n+1)
    arr[x] = 0
    pq = [(0, x)]
    def h(lst2, val2):
        i = 0
        j = len(lst2) - 1
        res = None
        while i <= j:
            k = (i + j) // 2
            if lst2[k] >= val2:
                res = lst2[k]
                j = k - 1
            else:
                i = k + 1
        return res
    c1 = 0
    c2 = 0
    c3 = 0
    while pq:
        t, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
        c2 += 1
        if t > arr[u]:
            continue
        if u == y:
            break
        for v, val, lst2 in A[u]:
            c1 += 1
            dt = h(lst2, t)
            if dt is None:
                continue
            at = dt + val
            if at < arr[v]:
                arr[v] = at
                c3 += 1
                heapq.heappush(pq, (at, v))
    res = arr[y] if arr[y] != INF else -1
    return res, {'binary_search_calls': c1, 'heap_extractions': c2, 'edge_relaxations': c3}

def f(n, m, x, y, lst):
    import heapq
    A = [[] for _ in range(n+1)]
    for a, b, val, lst2 in lst:
        lst2 = sorted(lst2)
        A[a].append((b, val, lst2))
    INF = float('inf')
    arr = [INF] * (n+1)
    arr[x] = 0
    pq = [(0, x)]
    def h(lst2, val2):
        i = 0
        j = len(lst2) - 1
        res = None
        while i <= j:
            k = (i + j) // 2
            if lst2[k] >= val2:
                res = lst2[k]
                j = k - 1
            else:
                i = k + 1
        return res
    c1 = 0
    c2 = 0
    c3 = 0
    while pq:
        t, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
        c2 += 1
        if t > arr[u]:

        if u == y:

        for v, val, lst2 in A[u]:
            c1 += 1
            dt = h(lst2, t)
            if dt is None:
                continue
            at = dt + val
            if at < arr[v]:

def f(n, m, x, y, lst):
    import heapq
    A = [[] for _ in range(n+1)]
    for a, b, val, lst2 in lst:
        lst2 = sorted(lst2)
        A[a].append((b, val, lst2))
    INF = float('inf')
    arr = [INF] * (n+1)
    arr[x] = 0
    pq = [(0, x)]
    def h(lst2, val2):
        i = 0
        j = len(lst2) - 1
        res = None
        while i <= j:
            k = (i + j) // 2
            if lst2[k] >= val2:
                res = lst2[k]
                j = k - 1
            else:
                i = k + 1
        return res
    c1 = 0
    c2 = 0
    c3 = 0
    while pq:
        t, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
        c2 += 1
        if t > arr[u]:
            continue
        if u == y:
            break
        for v, val, lst2 in A[u]:
            c1 += 1
            dt = h(lst2, t)
            if dt is None:
                continue
            at = dt + val
            if at < arr[v]:
                arr[v] = at
                c3 += 1
                heapq.heappush(pq, (at, v))

    return res, {'binary_search_calls': c1, 'heap_extractions': c2, 'edge_relaxations': c3}

def f(n, m, x, y, lst):
    import heapq
    A = [[] for _ in range(n+1)]
    for a, b, val, lst2 in lst:
        lst2 = sorted(lst2)
        A[a].append((b, val, lst2))
    INF = float('inf')
    arr = [INF] * (n+1)
    arr[x] = 0
    pq = [(0, x)]
    def h(lst2, val2):
        i = 0
        j = len(lst2) - 1
        res = None
        while i <= j:
            k = (i + j) // 2
            if lst2[k] >= val2:
                res = lst2[k]
                j = k - 1
            else:
                i = k + 1
        return res
    c1 = 0
    c2 = 0
    c3 = 0
    while pq:
        t, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
        c2 += 1
        if t > arr[u]:
            continue
        if u == y:
            break
        for v, val, lst2 in A[u]:
            c1 += 1
            dt = h(lst2, t)
            if dt is None:
                continue
            at = dt + val
            if at < arr[v]:
                arr[v] = at
                c3 += 1
                heapq.heappush(pq, (at, v))
    res = arr[y] if arr[y] != INF else -1
    return res, {'binary_search_calls': c1, 'heap_extractions': c2, 'edge_relaxations': c3}

def f(A, B):
    stats = {'subtractions': 0, 'comparisons': 0, 'cross_inv_events': 0}
    L = []
    for x, y in zip(A, B):
        L.append(x - y)
        stats['subtractions'] += 1
    def merge_count(arr):
        n = len(arr)
        if n <= 1:
            return arr, 0
        mid = n // 2
        arr1, inv1 = merge_count(arr[:mid])
        arr2, inv2 = merge_count(arr[mid:])
        lst = []
        i = j = 0
        inv = inv1 + inv2
        while i < len(arr1) and j < len(arr2):
            stats['comparisons'] += 1
            if arr1[i] <= arr2[j]:
                lst.append(arr1[i]); i += 1
            else:
                lst.append(arr2[j]); j += 1
                stats['cross_inv_events'] += 1
                inv += len(arr1) - i
        lst.extend(arr1[i:])
        lst.extend(arr2[j:])
        return lst, inv
    _, total = merge_count(L)
    return total, stats

Subtract y from x, append that result to the end of L, and then add 1 to stats['subtractions']. Do this until you’ve processed every pair and L has the same length as A.

Next, you define a little procedure called merge_count that takes any list arr and returns two things: a sorted version of arr and a count of how many inversion-like events it found inside. Here’s how merge_count works:

  1. Measure the length of arr and call it n.  
  2. If n is 0 or 1, you’re already done—just return arr itself and 0 (no inversions).  
  3. Otherwise, figure out mid = n divided by 2, rounded down.  
  4. Slice arr into two halves: arr1 is the first mid items (indices 0 through mid–1), and arr2 is the remaining items (indices mid through n–1).  
  5. Call merge_count recursively on arr1, which gives you a sorted arr1 plus a number inv1. Do the same on arr2 to get sorted arr2 and inv2.  
  6. Now set a local counter inv = inv1 + inv2, because any inversions inside each half have already been counted.  
  7. Create an empty list called lst, and set two pointers i = 0 and j = 0 to walk through sorted arr1 and sorted arr2.  
  8. While i < length of arr1 AND j < length of arr2, do this:  
     • Add 1 to stats['comparisons'] because you’re about to compare arr1[i] and arr2[j].  
     • If arr1[i] ≤ arr2[j], append arr1[i] to lst and add 1 to i.  
     • Otherwise, append arr2[j] to lst, add 1 to j, add 1 to stats['cross_inv_events'], and also add (length of arr1 – i) to inv, because every remaining item in arr1 from position i onward is inverted relative to arr2[j].  
  9. When that loop ends, one of the two lists has run out. Take any leftover slice of arr1 from i to the end and append all of it to lst in one go, then do the same with arr2 from j onward.  
 10. Now lst holds a fully merged, sorted list. Return lst and the current value of inv.

Back in your main flow, after you’ve built L, you call merge_count(L). That gives you two things: a sorted version of L (which you can ignore) and a number total, which is the sum of all inversion counts found during merging. Finally, you return total and the stats dictionary you created at the very start—stats now carries the totals of every subtraction, every comparison, and every cross-inversion event you counted along the way.

1. total – a single number that’s the overall count of inversion events produced by merge_count when sorting L.  
2. stats – a dictionary with three entries:

def f(A, B):
    stats = {'subtractions': 0, 'comparisons': 0, 'cross_inv_events': 0}
    L = []
    for x, y in zip(A, B):
        L.append(x - y)
        stats['subtractions'] += 1
    def merge_count(arr):
        n = len(arr)
        if n <= 1:
            return arr, 0
        mid = n // 2
        arr1, inv1 = merge_count(arr[:mid])
        arr2, inv2 = merge_count(arr[mid:])
        lst = []
        i = j = 0
        inv = inv1 + inv2
        while i < len(arr1) and j < len(arr2):
            stats['comparisons'] += 1
            if arr1[i] <= arr2[j]:
                lst.append(arr1[i]); i += 1
            else:
                lst.append(arr2[j]); j += 1
                stats['cross_inv_events'] += 1
                inv += len(arr1) - i
        lst.extend(arr1[i:])
        lst.extend(arr2[j:])
        return lst, inv
    _, total = merge_count(L)
    return total, stats

LOGICS: What you’re going to do is first look at arr and count its items, then call that count n. Next, you create two counters called pop_ops and max_updates, and set them to zero. Now, check whether n is less than 2; if it is, then you immediately know the result is zero and both counters stay at zero, so you stop right there. Otherwise, you set up another variable named val at zero and prepare an empty list called lst to hold indices. After that, you run a forward pass by letting an index i go from 0 to n minus one. At each i, start by looking at lst: while lst still has at least one entry and the number at arr at the last index stored in lst is smaller than arr at i, remove that last index from lst and add 1 to pop_ops. Keep repeating that removal until either lst is empty or the value at the stored index is no longer smaller than arr at i. When that popping is over, check if lst still has anything; if it does, compute cur by taking i minus the last index in lst minus one. If this cur is greater than the current val, replace val with cur and add 1 to max_updates. Finally, append the current i to lst and move on to the next i. Once you’ve handled every i from 0 up to n minus one, clear lst entirely so it’s empty again. Then you perform a backward pass by letting i run from n minus one down to 0. For each i in that downward sequence, repeat the exact same steps: while lst isn’t empty and arr at the last stored index is smaller than arr at i, pop that index off lst and add 1 to pop_ops; after popping, if lst still has an entry compute cur as lst’s last index minus i minus one and, if cur exceeds val, update val to cur and add 1 to max_updates; then append i to lst. When that backward loop finishes, you’re done. 

OUTPUTS: At the end you’ll have val as your main result, plus two counters in a small summary. pop_ops is the total number of times you removed an index from lst, and max_updates is how many times you found a larger gap and updated val.

LOGICS: Okay, here’s how you set up your desk and walk through every step by hand. First, you look at your list A and you need to know how many times each number appears. So you create a little tally sheet called B, where each unique number from A gets its own line and you write down its count. Next, write down all the unique numbers you’ve tallied, in order from smallest to largest—call that sorted strip of numbers lst. Then you look at the very last number in lst and call it n; that’s just the biggest number you have.

Now grab four blank counters and put them on your sheet: sum_trials = 0, pointer_iterations = 0, matches_found = 0, and res = 0. These will track what you do as you go.

What you’re going to do now is test every possible target sum x from 2 up to 2·n. So you start with x = 2. Each time you begin a new x, immediately add 1 to sum_trials—that’s keeping count of how many x’s you’ve tried.

After that, you’re looking for pairs of numbers from lst that add up exactly to this x. So set another counter called pairs = 0. Then place two markers: one at the start of lst (call its position i = 0) and one at the end of lst (call its position j = length of lst minus 1).

Now you do this dance while i is not past j (so while i ≤ j):
  • First thing inside the loop, add 1 to pointer_iterations. That’s marking every time you compare a pair.  
  • Then look at the numbers under those two markers: call the left number v1 = lst[i] and the right number v2 = lst[j].  
  • Add them together to get s = v1 + v2.  
  • If s is less than x, that means even the biggest v2 paired with v1 isn’t enough, so move your left marker one step to the right by doing i = i + 1.  
  • Otherwise, if s is greater than x, even the smallest v1 with v2 is too big, so move your right marker one step to the left by doing j = j - 1.  
  • Otherwise, s exactly equals x, which is what you want:
      – Right away add 1 to matches_found.  
      – Now you have to count how many actual pairs that sum gives you, based on how many copies of v1 and v2 you have in B.  
      – If your left marker and right marker are on different entries (i < j), you can pair each copy of the smaller with each copy of the bigger, but limited by whichever count is smaller. So do pairs = pairs + min(B[v1], B[v2]).  
      – If your markers meet in the middle on the exact same number (i == j), you have to pair up that number with itself, so each pair uses two copies. You can only make B[v1] // 2 pairs in that case. So do pairs = pairs + (B[v1] // 2).  
      – After counting, move both markers inward: i = i + 1 and j = j - 1.  

Keep repeating that while-loop until your left marker goes past your right marker (i > j). Once you’ve exhausted all pairs for this x, compare your pairs count to your best-so-far in res. If pairs is bigger than res, then replace res with pairs. That way res always holds the largest pairs count you’ve ever seen.

OUTPUTS: At the end, you’ll have two things: first, a single number called res, which is the biggest number of matching pairs you ever saw for any x; second, a little dictionary of three statistics:  
• sum_trials: how many x values you actually tried (that should be 2·n minus 1, since you go from 2 to 2·n),  
• pointer_iterations: how many times you compared a left and right entry in total,  
• matches_found: how many times you discovered a sum that matched exactly and did that pairing step.

   - You’ve got Q, a list of query triples, each triple written (a, b, c).

   - Go through A and jot down each distinct number on a scratch pad—no repeats.  
   - Once you’ve collected each distinct entry, sort those entries in ascending order.  Call that sorted list U.  

3. Record m, the length of U  
   - Count how many entries you have in U; that count is m.  

4. Create a mapping d from each value in U to a 1-based index  
   - Look at U[0], give it the label 1; look at U[1], give it label 2; … up to U[m−1] getting label m.  
   - On paper you now have pairs (value → its label). That’s your d.  

5. Compute mx, the maximum size for our working arrays  
   - Figure out how many bits it takes to write m in binary (that’s the bit_length of m).  
   - Add 2 to that bit_length.  
   - Multiply the result by n.  
   - Add 5.  
   - The final sum is mx.  

6. Allocate and initialize arrays and counters  
   - Create three arrays called B, C, S, each with indices from 0 up to mx−1, and fill every entry with 0.  
   - Create another array called roots with indices 0 through n, fill every entry with 0.  
   - On your sheet, note three counters: sz = 0, u_calls = 0, q_calls = 0.

   When you say update(p, l_, r_, v):  
   a. Add 1 to u_calls.  
   b. Add 1 to sz.  Let cur = the new value of sz.  
   c. Copy old slots into the new one:  
      - B[cur] = B[p]  
      - C[cur] = C[p]  
      - S[cur] = S[p] + 1  
   d. If l_ is less than r_, then:  
      i.  Compute mid = floor((l_ + r_) / 2)  
      ii. If v ≤ mid, do a recursive update on the left side:  
          • Call update(B[p], l_, mid, v), get back some index, and store it into B[cur].  
         Else (v > mid), do a recursive update on the right side:  
          • Call update(C[p], mid+1, r_, v), get back some index, and store it into C[cur].  
   e. Return cur.  

8. Define the query process (we’ll call it to answer one (a,b,c) query)  
   When you say query(p, q, l_, r_, k):  
   a. Add 1 to q_calls.  
   b. If l_ equals r_, return l_ immediately.  
   c. Otherwise, compute mid = floor((l_ + r_) / 2).

      • Return query(B[p], B[q], l_, mid, k).

      • Return query(C[p], C[q], mid+1, r_, k − cnt).

      • Append U[idx−1] to res.

    - At this point your list res holds one number per query, in the same order as Q.

That’s it—follow those steps in order and you’ll end up with exactly the same results as the code.

def f(arr, m):
    x = 0
    y = 0
    n = len(arr)
    if m >= n:
        return 0, {"cost_calls": x, "dp_updates": y}
    A = [0] + sorted(arr)
    B = [0] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        B[i] = B[i - 1] + A[i]
    def g(i, j):
        nonlocal x
        x += 1
        mid = (i + j) // 2
        v1 = A[mid] * (mid - i + 1) - (B[mid] - B[i - 1])
        v2 = (B[j] - B[mid]) - A[mid] * (j - mid)
        return v1 + v2
    INF = 10**18
    C = [INF] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        C[i] = g(1, i)
        y += 1
    C[0] = 0
    y += 1
    for t in range(2, m + 1):
        D = [INF] * (n + 1)
        for i in range(1, t):
            D[i] = 0
            y += 1
        def h(l, r, optl, optr):
            nonlocal y
            if l > r:
                return
            mid = (l + r) // 2
            best = INF
            opt = -1
            limit = min(optr, mid - 1)
            for j in range(optl, limit + 1):
                val = C[j] + g(j + 1, mid)
                if val < best:
                    best = val
                    opt = j
            D[mid] = best
            y += 1
            h(l, mid - 1, optl, opt)
            h(mid + 1, r, opt, optr)
        h(t, n, t - 1, n - 1)
        C = D
    return C[n], {"cost_calls": x, "dp_updates": y}

        v1 = A[mid] * (mid - i + 1) - (B[mid] - B[i - 1])

        return v1 + v2

def f(str1: str, str2: str) -> tuple[int, dict]:
    n = len(str1)
    A = [(int(str2[i]) - int(str1[i])) % 10 for i in range(n)]
    INF = float('inf')
    B = [[[INF] * 10 for _ in range(10)] for __ in range(n + 1)]
    B[0][0][0] = 0
    states_processed = 0
    updates = 0
    for i in range(n):
        for x in range(10):
            for y in range(10):
                c = B[i][x][y]
                if c == INF:
                    continue
                states_processed += 1
                need = (A[i] - x) % 10
                nr = (y + need) % 10
                nl = need
                if B[i + 1][nr][nl] > c + need:
                    B[i + 1][nr][nl] = c + need
                    updates += 1
                dec = (10 - need) % 10
                nr2 = (y - dec) % 10
                nl2 = (-dec) % 10
                if B[i + 1][nr2][nl2] > c + dec:
                    B[i + 1][nr2][nl2] = c + dec
                    updates += 1
    res = B[n][0][0]
    out = res if res < INF else -1
    return out, {"states_processed": states_processed, "updates": updates}

INPUTS: Two text strings str1 and str2 of equal length n, each made up of digit characters; a list A of length n containing integers between 0 and 9; a three-dimensional table B with dimensions (n+1)×10×10 holding numeric values; and two integer counters states_processed and updates. 

LOGICS: Start by figuring out n as the length of str1. Next, create an empty list called A. Now you’re going to fill that list by going through each position i from 0 up to n minus 1. At each i, take the character at position i in str2 and convert it to an integer, then take the character at the same position in str1 and convert that to an integer. Subtract the str1 number from the str2 number, then adjust it by adding or subtracting 10 until it falls into the range 0 through 9. Record that result in A at position i. Once you’ve done this for every i, A is a list of n numbers between 0 and 9. After that, define a symbol INF to stand for a huge number, effectively ‘infinity’. On paper you can just write INF or use a large number you know you’ll never beat. Now you need to set up a three-dimensional table called B. Imagine there are n+1 layers, and each layer is a 10×10 grid of cells. Fill every cell in every layer with INF. Label the layers from 0 up to n, and label the rows and columns in each layer from 0 through 9. After that, go to the cell at layer 0, row 0, column 0 and overwrite it with 0. Next, create two counters named states_processed and updates, and set them both to zero. At this point, you begin the main processing. For each layer index i going from 0 up to n minus 1, do the following. First you look at layer i in B. Then you loop through every possible row index x from 0 through 9, and for each x you loop through every column index y from 0 through 9. For each pair (x,y), read the value c in B at layer i, row x, column y. If c is equal to INF, skip the rest of the steps for this pair and move on to the next (y or x). If c is not INF, add 1 to your states_processed counter. Now calculate need as A[i] minus x, then adjust that result by adding or subtracting 10 until it falls between 0 and 9. That is need = (A[i] - x) modulo 10. Next you handle two options. First option: call it the forward action. Calculate nr as y plus need, then adjust by subtracting 10 if it’s 10 or more so it stays between 0 and 9. Then set nl equal to need. Now look at the cell in the next layer, B at layer i+1, row nr, column nl. If that cell currently holds a number bigger than c plus need, overwrite it with c plus need and add 1 to updates. Second option: call it the reverse action. Figure out dec by subtracting need from 10, then adjust by subtracting 10 if it’s 10 or more, giving a number between 0 and 9. That is dec = (10 - need) modulo 10. Compute nr2 by subtracting dec from y, then adjust by adding 10 if it becomes negative, so nr2 stays in 0 through 9. Compute nl2 by taking minus dec, then if that is negative add 10 so it’s also between 0 and 9. Now check B at layer i+1, row nr2, column nl2. If that value is bigger than c plus dec, overwrite it with c plus dec and add 1 to updates. Once you’ve done both options for the current (x,y) pair, move on until you’ve covered all y, then all x, then increase i by one and repeat until i reaches n minus 1. When that main loop finishes, you’ll be at layer n in B. Go to the cell at row 0, column 0 of that layer—that’s B[n][0][0]—and read its value. If it’s still INF, set your final result out to -1. Otherwise, out is simply that value. Finally, you return two things: the number out itself, and a little dictionary whose entries are states_processed (the total number of times you saw a finite cell and processed it) and updates (the total number of times you overwrote a cell with a smaller value). 

OUTPUTS: You end up with two pieces. The first is out, a single integer which is either the value from B[n][0][0] if it’s finite or -1 if that cell stayed at INF. The second is a dictionary with two entries: states_processed gives you how many states you actually processed (how often you saw a number that was not INF), and updates tells you how many times you found a smaller cost and updated a cell in the table.

def f(str1: str, str2: str) -> tuple[int, dict]:
    n = len(str1)
    A = [(int(str2[i]) - int(str1[i])) % 10 for i in range(n)]
    INF = float('inf')
    B = [[[INF] * 10 for _ in range(10)] for __ in range(n + 1)]
    B[0][0][0] = 0
    states_processed = 0
    updates = 0
    for i in range(n):
        for x in range(10):
            for y in range(10):
                c = B[i][x][y]
                if c == INF:
                    continue
                states_processed += 1
                need = (A[i] - x) % 10
                nr = (y + need) % 10
                nl = need
                if B[i + 1][nr][nl] > c + need:
                    B[i + 1][nr][nl] = c + need
                    updates += 1
                dec = (10 - need) % 10
                nr2 = (y - dec) % 10
                nl2 = (-dec) % 10
                if B[i + 1][nr2][nl2] > c + dec:
                    B[i + 1][nr2][nl2] = c + dec
                    updates += 1
    res = B[n][0][0]
    out = res if res < INF else -1
    return out, {"states_processed": states_processed, "updates": updates}

def f(str1: str, str2: str) -> tuple[int, dict]:
    n = len(str1)
    A = [(int(str2[i]) - int(str1[i])) % 10 for i in range(n)]
    INF = float('inf')
    B = [[[INF] * 10 for _ in range(10)] for __ in range(n + 1)]
    B[0][0][0] = 0
    states_processed = 0
    updates = 0
    for i in range(n):
        for x in range(10):
            for y in range(10):
                c = B[i][x][y]
                if c == INF:
                    continue
                states_processed += 1
                need = (A[i] - x) % 10
                nr = (y + need) % 10
                nl = need
                if B[i + 1][nr][nl] > c + need:
                    B[i + 1][nr][nl] = c + need
                    updates += 1
                dec = (10 - need) % 10
                nr2 = (y - dec) % 10
                nl2 = (-dec) % 10
                if B[i + 1][nr2][nl2] > c + dec:
                    B[i + 1][nr2][nl2] = c + dec
                    updates += 1
    res = B[n][0][0]
    out = res if res < INF else -1
    return out, {"states_processed": states_processed, "updates": updates}
